# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and pharmacological rationale

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity, mortality, and hospitalization worldwide. For decades, inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system formed the cornerstone of pharmacotherapy for HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The dual molecule sacubitril/valsartan represents the first agent in the class of angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI), combining the angiotensin receptor blocker valsartan with the neprilysin inhibitor sacubitril [1]. Inhibition of neprilysin augments natriuretic peptides, which defend the heart against volume and pressure overload; because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, the strategy combines a neprilysin inhibitor with an angiotensin-receptor blocker [2]. This complementary mechanism potentiates natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic effects while blocking the maladaptive effects of angiotensin II [3].

## Pivotal evidence in HFrEF: PARADIGM-HF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established the efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in chronic HFrEF. In this double-blind trial, 8442 patients with class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less were randomly assigned to receive either LCZ696 (200 mg twice daily) or enalapril (10 mg twice daily), in addition to recommended therapy [4]. The study was stopped prematurely after a mean follow-up of 27 months, due to the overwhelming clinical benefit of sacubitril/valsartan over enalapril found in a pre-specified interim analysis [5]. A total of 711 patients (17.0%) receiving LCZ696 and 835 (19.8%) receiving enalapril died (hazard ratio 0.84); LCZ696 also reduced the risk of hospitalization for heart failure by 21% and decreased symptoms and physical limitations [4].

The mortality benefit was driven by reductions in distinct modes of death. Further analysis showed a reduction in both death due to worsening heart failure ('pump failure') and sudden cardiac death, and sudden cardiac death was reduced to a similar extent in patients with and without an implantable cardioverter defibrillator [6]. Sacubitril/valsartan also slowed clinical progression: fewer LCZ696-treated patients required intensification of medical treatment for heart failure or an emergency department visit for worsening heart failure [7]. A post-hoc analysis demonstrated that benefit was maintained even among patients requiring dose reductions, with 42% of those randomized to sacubitril/valsartan and 43% of those randomized to enalapril undergoing a dose reduction [8]. Importantly, benefit persisted across subgroups, including in stable patients without recent decompensation [9] and similarly in women and men [10]. Even in patients experiencing hypotension, the benefits of sacubitril/valsartan were maintained or even enhanced [11].

## Mechanistic insights and reverse remodeling

The mechanisms underlying clinical benefit have been clarified by biomarker and imaging studies. In the PROVE-HF study, treatment with sacubitril/valsartan reduces NT-proBNP concentrations in HFrEF, though the effect on cardiac remodeling had been uncertain [12]. Reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months, providing evidence of reverse cardiac remodeling [12]. These observations support neprilysin inhibition as a contributor to structural and functional recovery beyond renin–angiotensin blockade alone [13].

## Acute and post-discharge initiation

The PIONEER-HF trial extended the evidence to hospitalized patients. Whether initiation of sacubitril–valsartan is safe and effective among patients hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure had been unknown; the trial enrolled patients with HFrEF hospitalized for acute decompensated heart failure [14]. In-hospital initiation produced greater NT-proBNP reduction and, in exploratory analysis, fewer clinical events without excess adverse events [15]. The TRANSITION study complemented this by showing that sacubitril/valsartan can be safely initiated early after decompensation requiring hospitalization, comparing pre- versus post-discharge initiation in HFrEF patients [16].

## Preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction

The earlier phase 2 PARAMOUNT trial showed that in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, LCZ696 reduced NT-proBNP to a greater extent than did valsartan at 12 weeks and was well tolerated [17]. However, the definitive PARAGON-HF trial was neutral: sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes among patients with an ejection fraction of 45% or higher [18]. A subgroup with LVEF below the median 57% value displayed a significant reduction, suggesting benefit concentrated at lower ejection fractions [19]. The PARAGLIDE-HF trial and a pooled analysis with PARAGON-HF reinforced this signal; in pooled analyses, sacubitril/valsartan reduced cardiovascular and renal events among patients with HF with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction [20,21].

## Post-myocardial infarction

The PARADISE-MI trial tested whether benefit extended to acute myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction. Sacubitril–valsartan was not associated with a significantly lower incidence of death from cardiovascular causes or incident heart failure than ramipril among patients with acute myocardial infarction [22]. Treated patients experienced 6.7 events per 100 patient-years versus 7.4 for ramipril, a hazard ratio of 0.90 (95% CI 0.78–1.04) [23]. This builds on the foundational VALIANT trial of renin–angiotensin blockade after MI [24].

## Guidelines and implementation

Current guidelines endorse ARNI as a foundational therapy. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline includes new treatment strategies including ARNI and SGLT2 inhibitors [25], while the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend ARNI to replace ACE inhibitors in suitable HFrEF patients [26]. Despite these recommendations, implementation remains incomplete. Although guidelines strongly recommend multiple proven medications, the degree to which gaps in medication use and dosing persist in contemporary outpatient practice is unclear [27], and registries such as CHAMP-HF documented low ARNI uptake and frequent sub-target dosing [28,29]. Long-term open-label extension data have continued to support the safety and tolerability of sacubitril/valsartan [30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed the management of HFrEF, reducing mortality, hospitalizations, and sudden death, with mechanistic support from reverse remodeling data. Its role is more nuanced across the ejection fraction spectrum—greatest at lower ejection fractions—and it offers no clear advantage in the acute post-MI setting. Optimizing real-world implementation and dosing remains a priority for translating trial benefits into population-level outcomes.
